growth_story.headline: Aruba's income per person slid through the 2009 crisis and a refinery shutdown, then a post-pandemic tourism boom carried it to a record in 2024.
growth_story.arc: Since 1990, Aruba's income per person has moved through three eras: growth of 1.3 percent a year in 1990–2004, a fall of 1.9 percent a year in 2005–2012, and growth of 2.9 percent a year in 2013–2024. The IMF ties the middle era to a double-dip recession caused by the global financial crisis and the shutdown of the oil refinery, and income per person fell 12.3 percent in 2009 alone. Growth came back after 2013 but stayed uneven: the IMF described a gradual recovery, weak tourism in 2016 and hopes resting on a refinery reopening. The pandemic cut income per person by 23.5 percent in 2020, and a tourism-driven rebound followed, with growth of 15.8, 11.0, 9.5 and 6.2 percent from 2021 to 2024. That rebound lifted the 10-year average to 3.0 percent a year, against -0.5 in the decade before, and income per person reached its highest level yet in 2024. The IMF now expects growth to slow as tourism and hotel investment ease, and it says strong tourism demand is straining housing, workers and infrastructure.

threads.title: Refinery shutdown and global crisis
threads.text: Aruba's oil refinery closed in July 2009 as tourism fell after the global downturn. The IMF later called the result a double-dip recession, which matches the 2005–2012 era when income per person fell 1.9 percent a year.

threads.text: After 2013 the IMF described a gradual recovery, held back in 2016 by weak tourism and shrinking non-tourism exports. Officials expected a refinery reopening to lift the economy; the sources here do not say whether it reopened.

threads.title: Pandemic collapse, tourism rebound
threads.text: Income per person fell 23.5 percent in 2020. Tourists returned once pandemic restrictions were lifted, and four years of strong growth took income per person to a record in 2024.

threads.title: Public debt up, then down
threads.text: Public debt climbed during the slow years after the 2009 crisis and was higher still in 2020. The IMF reports that it has fallen sharply since then.

citations.title: Kingdom of the Netherlands—Aruba: Concluding Statement of the 2015 Article IV Mission
citations.quote: Public debt surpassed 80 percent of GDP in 2014.

citations.title: Kingdom of the Netherlands-Aruba: Staff Concluding Statement of the 2025 Article IV Mission
citations.quote: Central government debt declined from 116.3 percent of GDP in 2020 to 68.6 percent by end-2024.

threads.title: Limits of a tourism economy
threads.text: Recent growth has come from tourism, and the IMF says strong tourism demand is now straining housing, workers and infrastructure. The 2025 IMF statement also names other sectors, such as agriculture and creative industries, in the discussion of where growth could come from.

citations.title: IMF Executive Board Concludes 2025 Article IV Consultation Discussions with The Kingdom of the Netherlands—Aruba
citations.quote: Strong tourism demand is straining infrastructure, labor markets, and housing availability and affordability

citations.title: Kingdom of the Netherlands-Aruba: Staff Concluding Statement of the 2025 Article IV Mission
citations.quote: Promote "Promising Sectors": agriculture, circular economy, creative industries, knowledge economy

since_last_year.text: In December 2025 the IMF said the tourism-driven boom is set to slow, as tourism and hotel investment ease after four strong years.

citations.title: IMF Executive Board Concludes 2025 Article IV Consultation Discussions with The Kingdom of the Netherlands—Aruba
citations.quote: Growth is projected to slow to about 4.0 percent in 2025 as tourism and hotel investments ease

growth_story.tension: In 2017 the IMF reported that the economy shrank in 2015 and 2016, but the data show income per person growing 2.6 percent in 2015 and 0.5 percent in 2016. The sources do not explain the gap.
